source_text: νοητὰ τοῖς τῆς ὕλης ῥεύμασιν συνεξομοιοῦσθαι νομίζοντες. 16.2 τὰ μὲν γὰρ ὑπερουράνια πάντα νοῦν καὶ πᾶσαν νόησιν ὑπερβαίνοντα, τὰ δὲ γήϊνα καὶ ταπεινὰ καὶ χρόνῳ γινόμενα καὶ ἀπογινόμενα τυγχάνει. 16.3 Ἀλλὰ μάλιστα μὲν ἀνάρχως 14 ἐτέχθη, συνυπάρχων καὶ συμπράττων τῷ ἑαυτοῦ ἀληθινῷ πατρί, ὡς τὸ φῶς τῷ ἡλιακῷ δίσκῳ. 16.4 ἔχει δὲ τὸ εἶναι καὶ ἀπὸ γραφῶν μαρτυρεῖσθαι θεός, κύριος, ἅγιος, δημιουργός, ἄφθαρτος, ζωή, φῶς καὶ πάντα ὅσα ὁ πατήρ. 16.5 καὶ μᾶλλον ἐκ τῶν πλειόνων τὸ ὅμοιον καὶ ἴσον ἔχειν ὀφείλει ἤπερ ἀπὸ τοῦ ἑνὸς τὸ ἀνόμοιον. 16.6 Πῶς δὲ ὁ Ἀδὰμ καὶ ἡ Εὔα οὐ γεννηθέντες οὐδὲ πατέρα ἐσχηκότες τοῖς ἐξ αὐτῶν ἡμῖν ἴσοι τῇ φύσει γεγόνασιν; 16.7 ἢ ποίαν ἁπλῶς παράθεσιν ποιησάμενοι τοῦ ὡς λέγουσιν ἀνομοίου ἢ πῶς παραμετρήσαντες ἐπέστησαν τῷ «κρείττονι καὶ μείζονι»; γραφῆς μὲν οὔτε διοριζούσης τῇ φύσει τὴν ἁγίαν καὶ ἄναρχον μίαν καὶ ἀμέριστον τριάδα, οὐδ' αὖ πάλιν ἀφοριζούσης αὐτῇ τὸ πρώτιστα καὶ τὸ ἔπειτα; 16.8 δήλων δὲ ὄντων δύο τούτων, ὅτι τε οὐ πάντως τὸ μεῖζον ἑτεροούσιόν ἐστι, καὶ ὅτι καθ' ὅλου τὰ συγκριτικὰ ἐπὶ ὁμοουσίων, ἀλλ' οὐκ ἐπὶ ἑτεροουσίων λέγεται. 16.9 οὐκ ἂν δὲ οὐδ' ἐξ ἐπιβολῆς εἴποιεν καίριον, ὅτι οὐδὲ περὶ τοῦ «ἀσυγκρίτου καὶ μείζονος». 16.10 Οὐ κατὰ μέγεθος ἤ τινα ὄγκον· ἀμεγέθης γὰρ καὶ ἀπλατής ἐστιν καὶ πηλικότητος πάσης καὶ συνθέσεως καὶ σχήματος ἀναχωρήσας ὁ θεὸς λόγος, καθὰ καὶ ὁ πατὴρ καὶ τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα αὐτοῦ, καὶ ὑπὸ μηδενὸς μὲν περιεχόμενος αὐτός, πάντα δὲ ἐμπεριέχων. 16.11 διότι καὶ πάντων ἀρχὴ μεγεθῶν ὡς ποιητής ἐστιν. ποῦ γὰρ ἐν ταῖς ἀκροτάταις καὶ ὑπερασωμάτοις καὶ κρείττοσιν ὑποστάσεσιν μέγεθος; 16.12 Οὐδὲ κατὰ τὸ ἄναρχον. συνυπάρχει γὰρ τῷ πατρὶ ὡς «ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ» καὶ μὴ ἔχων πρὸ αὐτοῦ θεόν. 16.13 καὶ γάρ φησιν· «ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος». καὶ οὐδὲ συμμετρεῖται χρόνῳ θεὸς καὶ ποιητὴς ποιήματι. 16.14 ἐπεὶ ἀνάγκη αὐτοὺς ἀπαιτεῖ– ὅπερ καὶ ἐννοεῖν σφαλερόν–πρότερον ὑποστῆσαι τοῦ ἀνάρχου καὶ ἀπερινοήτου θεοῦ καὶ πατρὸς χρόνον καὶ οὕτω συγκρίνειν. 16.15 ἄνθρωποι δὲ εἰώθασι «μείζονας» καλεῖν τοὺς χρόνῳ τὴν γένεσιν προειληφότας, κατὰ τὸν Ἰσαὰκ διαταττόμενον· «ὁ μείζων δουλεύσει τῷ ἐλάττονι». 16.16 Οὐδὲ ὡς αἴτιος. οὐ γὰρ αἴτιος αὐτοῦ. ἄναρχος γὰρ καὶ ὁ μονογενὴς υἱὸς ἐδείχθη· ἐπεὶ ὁμοίως αὐτοῦ τε καὶ ἡμῶν μείζων, ὅπερ μὴ γένοιτο εἰπεῖν ἢ ἀκοῦσαι. 16.17 Οὐδὲ κατὰ τὴν οὐσίαν καὶ τὸ ὅμοιον. ἐξ αὐτοῦ γάρ «ὡς μονογενὴς παρὰ πατρός, πλήρης χάριτος καὶ ἀληθείας», καὶ ὡς «χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως» πρὸς ἅπαντα ὢν χαρακτὴρ, καὶ ὡς «εἰκὼν τοῦ θεοῦ», ἣν «ὁ ἑωρακὼς ἑώρακε τὸν πατέρα». «ἐν αὐτῷ γὰρ κατοι κεῖ πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος». 16.18 ἐπισπᾶται δὲ τοῦτο μαρτυρίᾳ καὶ τὸ «ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον κατ' εἰκόνα καὶ ὁμοίωσιν ἡμετέραν». 16.19 Οὐδὲ κατὰ ποιότητος ἐπίτασιν, ἐπεὶ μὴ ποιότητες αἱ θεῖαι καὶ ἀπόρρητοι ὑποστάσεις· ἐν σώμασι γὰρ ἡ ποιότης· αἱ δὲ ἀσώματοι καὶ νοηταί. 16.20 Ἀλλὰ μηδὲ νοεῖσθαι δύναται περὶ αὐτῶν, ὡς εἴη τοῦ καλοῦ κάλλιον καὶ τοῦ καλλίονος βέλτιον, παραπλησίως τῇ περὶ ἄλλου λεγούσῃ Παύλου φωνῇ· «νυνὶ δὲ μένει τὰ τρία ταῦτα· πίστις, ἐλπίς, ἀγάπη· μείζων δὲ τούτων ἡ ἀγάπη». 16.21 διὰ γὰρ τὴν εἰς ἀρετὴν ἐπίτασιν ἀπένειμεν τῇ ἀγάπῃ τὸ «μείζων». ἀγαπήσαντες γάρ, φησί, πιστεύομεν καὶ πιστεύσαντες ἐλπίζομεν συμβασιλεῦσαι τῷ Χριστῷ. 16.22 εἰ γὰρ ἀληθὲς τό «εἷς θέος» καὶ τό «ἵνα γένησθε θείας κοινωνοὶ φύσεως» καὶ οὐχί· φύσεων, ἓν εἶναι καὶ τὸ καθάπαξ καλὸν ἀποδέδεικται, φημὶ δέ· ἡ θεότης. 16.23 Οὐδὲ κατὰ τὸ ἴσον, διότι μέγας καί «ἐπὶ πάντων» γέγραπται, «θεός» ὁ υἱός, «ἴσον ἑαυτὸν ποιῶν τῷ πατρί» καί «ὀμνύων καθ' ἑαυτοῦ, ἐπειδὴ μὴ ἔχει τὸν μείζονα». 16.24 Οὐδὲ κατὰ τὴν δύναμιν. γέγραπται γάρ· «Χριστὸν θεοῦ δύναμιν καὶ θεοῦ σοφίαν», καί «πάντα ὅσα ἂν ποιῇ ὁ πατὴρ καὶ ὁ υἱὸς ὁμοίως ποιεῖ». 16.25 Οὐδὲ κατὰ τὴν δόξαν ἤ τι ἀξίωμα. «εἰ γὰρ ᾔδεσαν», φησίν, «οὐκ ἂν τὸν κύριον τῆς δόξης ἐσταύρωσαν». καὶ θέλημά ἐστιν τοῦ πατρὸς κατὰ τὸν Ἰωάννην, «ἵνα πάντες τιμῶσι τὸν υἱόν, καθὼς τιμῶσι τὸν πατέρα». 16.26 κατὰ τί οὖν λοιπὸν τὸ μείζω καὶ ἀνόμοιον; ὡς ἐδείχθη, κατ' οὐδέν. 16.27 καὶ γοῦν ὁ ἀπόστολος τὰς εἰς τὸν μονογενῆ υἱὸν καὶ θεὸν ἀσεβεῖς ὑπολήψει αἱρετικῶν ἀναστέλλων, τὴν δὲ πρὸς τὸν πατέρα αὐτοῦ τῆς φύσεως ταυτότητα ἔτι δὲ 15 καὶ τὸ συνάναρχον κηρύττων, γράψας, ὡς ἀνωτέρω ἐλέχθη· «ὃς ὢν ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης τοῦ πατρός» ἐπήγαγεν· «καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ». 16.28 καὶ
pass_a_gloss: [... and the] intelligible things, thinking they are made alike together with the flowings of matter. 16.2 For the things above the heavens all surpass mind and every thought, while the earthly things happen to be both lowly and coming to be and ceasing to be in time. 16.3 But above all he was brought forth without beginning, existing together and acting together with his own true Father, as the light with the disc of the sun. 16.4 And he has his being attested also from the Scriptures as God, Lord, holy, Creator, incorruptible, life, light, and all things as many as the Father [is]. 16.5 And he ought rather to have the like and equal from the more [things] than from the one the unlike. 16.6 And how have Adam and Eve, not having been begotten nor having had a father, become equal in nature to us who are from them? 16.7 Or what comparison at all having made of the, as they say, unlike, or how having measured alongside did they fix upon the 'better and greater'? while Scripture neither divides by nature the holy and beginningless one and undivided Trinity, nor again marks off for it the first-of-all and the afterwards? 16.8 And these two things being plain: both that the greater is not necessarily of another substance, and that in general the comparative [words] are said of things of the same substance, but not of things of other substance. 16.9 And they would not even by guesswork say anything apt, since not even about the 'incomparable and greater'. 16.10 Not according to size or some bulk: for the God Word is sizeless and breadthless, and has withdrawn from all magnitude and composition and shape, just as also the Father and his Holy Spirit, and he himself is encompassed by nothing, but encompasses all things. 16.11 Because he is also beginning of all magnitudes as maker. For where in the topmost and beyond-incorporeal and superior hypostases [is] magnitude? 16.12 Nor according to the beginningless. For he exists together with the Father as 'radiance of his glory' and not having God before him. 16.13 For indeed it says: 'in the beginning was the Word'. And God and maker is not measured together by time with a made thing. 16.14 Since necessity demands of them — which is perilous even to think — to posit a time before the beginningless and incomprehensible God and Father and so to compare. 16.15 And men are accustomed to call 'greater' those who have taken the lead in birth by time, according to Isaac ordaining: 'the greater will serve the lesser'. 16.16 Nor as cause. For he is not his cause. For the only-begotten Son too has been shown beginningless; since [else he would be] alike greater than him and us, which may it not happen to say or to hear. 16.17 Nor according to the substance and the like. For [he is] from him 'as only-begotten from a father, full of grace and truth', and as 'stamp of the hypostasis', being a stamp toward all things, and as 'image of God', which 'the one who has seen has seen the Father'. 'For in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead'. 16.18 And this draws in for testimony also the 'let us make man according to image and our likeness'. 16.19 Nor according to intensification of quality, since the divine and unspeakable hypostases are not qualities; for quality [is] in bodies, but they [are] bodiless and intelligible. 16.20 But it cannot even be thought about them that there be [something] more beautiful than the beautiful and better than the more beautiful, nearly like the voice of Paul speaking about another thing: 'and now remain these three: faith, hope, love; and greater of these the love'. 16.21 For on account of the intensification toward virtue he allotted to love the 'greater'. For having loved, he says, we believe, and having believed we hope to reign together with Christ. 16.22 For if true is the 'one God' and the 'that you may become sharers of divine nature', and not: of natures, it has been shown that also the good once for all is one, and I say: the Godhead. 16.23 Nor according to the equal, because the Son has been written great and 'over all' 'God', 'making himself equal to the Father' and 'swearing by himself, since he does not have the greater'. 16.24 Nor according to the power. For it has been written: 'Christ power of God and wisdom of God', and 'all things whatever the Father does, the Son also does likewise'. 16.25 Nor according to the glory or some rank. 'For if they had known,' it says, 'they would not have crucified the Lord of the glory'. And it is will of the Father according to John 'that all honour the Son as they honour the Father'. 16.26 According to what then still [is] the greater and unlike? As was shown, according to nothing. 16.27 And so the apostle, checking the impious suppositions of heretics about the only-begotten Son and God, and proclaiming the sameness of nature toward his Father and further also the being-together-without-beginning, having written, as was said higher up: 'who being radiance of the glory of the Father', brought on: 'and stamp of his hypostasis'. 16.28 And [...]
pass_b_english: … intelligible realities, supposing that they are made like the flux of matter. For the things above the heavens all surpass every mind and every thought, while earthly things are lowly, and come to be and pass away in time.

But above all, he was born without beginning, co-existing and co-working with his own true Father, as light with the disc of the sun. And he has the witness of the Scriptures that he is God, Lord, holy, Creator, incorruptible, life, light, and everything that the Father is. And he ought rather to be granted likeness and equality from the many than unlikeness from the one.

And how did Adam and Eve, who were not begotten and had no father, come to be equal in nature to us who are descended from them? Or what comparison at all did they make of what they call ‘unlike’? Or by what measuring did they settle on ‘better and greater’, when Scripture neither divides by nature the holy, beginningless, one and undivided Trinity, nor marks off within it a first and a later? Two things are plain: that what is greater is not necessarily of another substance, and that comparatives, as a rule, are used of things of the same substance, not of things of different substance. Nor could they say anything to the point even by guesswork, since they cannot do so even about ‘incomparable and greater’.

It is not by size or any bulk. For God the Word is without size or breadth, and stands apart from all magnitude, composition and shape, as do the Father and his Holy Spirit; he himself is contained by nothing, but contains all things. For he is also the beginning of all magnitudes, as their maker. Where indeed is there size in the highest and superior hypostases, which are beyond even the incorporeal?

Nor is it in respect of being without beginning. For he co-exists with the Father as “the radiance of his glory” (Hebrews 1:3), and has no God before him. For indeed it says: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1). And God, the Maker, is not measured by time alongside a thing made. For necessity demands of them, a thing perilous even to think, that they posit a time before the God and Father who is without beginning and beyond comprehension, and so make the comparison. People are accustomed to call ‘greater’ those who were born earlier in time, as when Isaac ordains: “The greater shall serve the lesser” (Genesis 25:23).

Nor is it as cause: for he is not his cause. For the only-begotten Son too has been shown to be without beginning; otherwise the Father would be greater than him in the same way as he is greater than us, which be it far from us to say or to hear.

Nor is it in substance and likeness. For he is from him “as the Only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14), and as “the stamp of his hypostasis” (Hebrews 1:3), a stamp in every respect, and as “the image of God” (2 Corinthians 4:4; Colossians 1:15), of which it is said that “he who has seen it has seen the Father” (John 14:9). “For in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead” (Colossians 2:9). And the words “Let us make man after our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26) are also drawn in as witness to this.

Nor is it by a heightening of quality, since the divine and ineffable hypostases are not qualities. Quality is found in bodies, but they are incorporeal and intelligible. Indeed, it cannot even be thought of them that there is something more beautiful than the beautiful and better than the more beautiful, in the manner of Paul’s saying on another matter: “And now these three remain: faith, hope, love; but the greater of these is love” (1 Corinthians 13:13). For he assigned ‘greater’ to love because of its intensity toward virtue: having loved, he says, we believe, and having believed we hope to reign with Christ.

For if “one God” (1 Corinthians 8:6) is true, and “that you may become partakers of the divine nature” (2 Peter 1:4), not ‘of natures’, then it has been shown that the good, taken absolutely, is also one: I mean the Godhead.

Nor is it in respect of equality, because it is written that the Son is great and “God over all” (Romans 9:5), “making himself equal to the Father” (John 5:18), and “swearing by himself, since he has no one greater” (Hebrews 6:13).

Nor is it in power. For it is written: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), and “Whatever the Father does, the Son also does likewise” (John 5:19). Nor is it in glory or any rank. “For if they had known,” it says, “they would not have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8). And it is the Father’s will, according to John, “that all should honour the Son just as they honour the Father” (John 5:23).

In what respect, then, does ‘greater’ and ‘unlike’ still hold? As has been shown, in none. And so the Apostle, checking the impious suppositions of heretics about the only-begotten Son and God, and proclaiming his identity of nature with his Father and, moreover, that he is equally without beginning, wrote, as was said above, “who, being the radiance of the glory of the Father,” and went on: “and the stamp of his hypostasis” (Hebrews 1:3).
notes: Khazarzar; Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify

choices.issue: Old draft a run-together digest with a false break
choices.choice: Retranslated the whole section from the Greek. The old English ran 16.1-16.16 into one paragraph, then wrote '[Text ends abruptly]' after 'Nor as a cause', though the Greek continues without a break. It read ἄναρχος (without beginning) as 'unbegotten' in 16.7 and 16.12, ἀπλατής (without breadth) as 'simplicity', ἀπαύγασμα as 'emanation', ἑτεροούσιον as a transliteration, ᾔδεσαν (they had known) as 'if we had known', made the Son 'greater than both himself and us' (16.16: the Father would be greater than the Son as he is than us), made love 'gain' the greater (16.21: Paul assigned it), and made the Apostle 'prevent the identity of nature' (16.27: he proclaimed it). 16.5 and 16.9 were garbled. References: 'making himself equal to the Father' was given Philippians 2:6, corrected to John 5:18 (Philippians 2:6 reads 'equal with God'); Hebrews 1:3 added at 16.12, 16.17 and 16.27, Genesis 25:23 for 'the greater shall serve the lesser', 2 Corinthians 4:4 and Colossians 1:15 for 'the image of God'. Bracket fillers '[the Son]', '[is he greater]' (five times), '[in terms of comparison]', '[preventing]' removed.

choices.term: νοητὰ τοῖς τῆς ὕλης ῥεύμασιν συνεξομοιοῦσθαι νομίζοντες
choices.english: … intelligible realities, supposing that they are made like the flux of matter
choices.why: The section opens inside the sentence of 16.1 (… καὶ τά): the opponents drag divine things down to the conditions of our nature. Only the words this section holds are translated, with a leading ellipsis.
The 'one' is the single point of being begotten (16.1); the 'many' are the shared titles of 16.4. Kept as terse as Didymus has it.

choices.term: οὐκ ἂν δὲ οὐδ' ἐξ ἐπιβολῆς εἴποιεν καίριον, ὅτι οὐδὲ περὶ τοῦ «ἀσυγκρίτου καὶ μείζονος»
choices.english: Nor could they say anything to the point even by guesswork, since they cannot do so even about ‘incomparable and greater’
choices.why: Elliptical clause; the verb 'say' is understood again after ὅτι οὐδέ. It introduces the list that follows (not by size, not by beginning, not as cause …), which shows there is no sense in which 'greater' fits.

choices.term: ἐπεὶ ἀνάγκη αὐτοὺς ἀπαιτεῖ … πρότερον ὑποστῆσαι … χρόνον
choices.english: For necessity demands of them … that they posit a time before
choices.why: A comparison in time would require time before the Father; ἐπεί kept as a plain 'for'.

choices.term: ἐπεὶ ὁμοίως αὐτοῦ τε καὶ ἡμῶν μείζων
choices.english: otherwise the Father would be greater than him in the same way as he is greater than us
choices.why: Elliptical 'otherwise' clause; the subject is the Father of the whole list. 'the Father' is named because English 'he' would be unclear after 'the Son'.

choices.english: for he is not his cause
choices.why: Translated as it stands: Didymus denies that the Father is greater as a cause that comes before an effect, since the Son is without beginning.

choices.term: χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως … πρὸς ἅπαντα ὢν χαρακτήρ
choices.english: the stamp of his hypostasis … a stamp in every respect
choices.why: χαρακτήρ is the impress of a seal; 'hypostasis' kept as Didymus' Trinitarian term.

choices.term: ἣν ὁ ἑωρακὼς ἑώρακε τὸν πατέρα
choices.english: of which it is said that “he who has seen it has seen the Father”
choices.why: Didymus fits John 14:9 to the image (ἥν), so 'it' replaces John's 'me'; 'it is said' marks the quotation.
More or less of a quality; Didymus denies the hypostases are qualities that admit degrees.

choices.english: but the greater of these is love
choices.why: Kept as 'greater' (not 'greatest') because Didymus' argument turns on the word μείζων.
καθάπαξ 'once for all, absolutely': the one good is the one Godhead.
The two words fit several verses (1 Corinthians 8:6, Ephesians 4:6, 1 Timothy 2:5); the reference the old draft gave is kept, since it reads 'one God'.
Read as the plural ὑπολήψεις, agreeing with τὰς … ἀσεβεῖς.
Printed line numbers 14 and 15 inside the Greek are page debris and are skipped.
Word split by a line break in the copy-text; read as κατοικεῖ.
